question: The Green Deal promotes a policy based on the use of renewable energy sources, like solar and wind power, and electric cars. This makes Europe now dependent on China, which dominates the global electric car battery market and accounts for 80 % of global solar panel production, all while violating workers’ fundamental rights and without complying with the EU’s strict environmental standards.

Recently, the Commission itself launched an anti-subsidy investigation into the import of battery electric vehicles from China (to determine whether illegal subsidisation is happening, which could cause economic injury to EU manufacturers), and an inquiry into suspected subsidies for Chinese solar panel and wind turbine producers (as it appears that they are receiving subsidies, which is distorting the internal market, with Chinese wind turbines costing up to 50 % less than EUmanufactured turbines).
In view of the above: 1.
Will the Commission carry out an impact assessment on the supply of these raw materials required for the green policies pushed for by the Commission?
What action will it take to mitigate the risk of the EU being overly reliant on China?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.6.2024) The Commission has a comprehensive approach to achieve a secure and sustainable supply of critical raw materials (CRM) for the green and digital transition, as set out in Commission Communication COM(2023) 165 final1. When the Commission proposed the Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA), now adopted2, it was accompanied by an impact assessment report3.

The CRMA contains measures to support the building up of domestic capacities along the CRM value chain. The Commission’s approach also seeks to overcome strategic dependencies by diversifying the EU supply and improving transparency of supply and demand, in order to assess and mitigate risks of vulnerabilities.

This is pursued by cooperating with trading partners both bilaterally and multilaterally, for example, through bilateral discussions on supply chains under the EU’s Trade and Technology Councils with the United States and with India, and engagement in multilateral fora such as the World Trade Organization.

This approach will facilitate addressing these weaknesses and enhancing the resilience of the global trading system. The Commission also promotes the uptake of the circular economy to reduce overall demand of these materials and ramping up of domestic industry.

For innovating and scaling up the manufacturing capacity of net-zero technologies in the EU, the Commission presented in March 2023 a proposal for a Net-Zero Industry Act (NZIA)4. This initiative contains a series of measures aiming at addressing strategic dependencies and enhancing resilience in support of the green transition, notably for the solar and wind sectors.
The European Parliament and the Council concluded the negotiations on a compromise text for the NZIA on 6 February 20245.
